lesson_1.topicLabel: Enquiry 01: Roman Law, Twelve Tables and Bath Curse Tablets (AD 43–410)
lesson_1.title: How did the Romans catch thieves and judge crimes without police?
lesson_1.spokenTitle: How did the Romans catch thieves and judge crimes without police?

cards.heading: Twelve Tables & Basilica Courts
cards.connective: How did the Romans catch thieves and judge crimes without police?
cards.html: After AD 43, Rome brought written rules rooted in the Twelve Tables. Town magistrates weighed witness proof inside grand stone basilicas.
cards.spoken: How did the Romans catch thieves and judge crimes without police? <short pause> After AD 43, Rome brought written rules rooted in the Twelve Tables. Town magistrates weighed witness proof inside grand stone basilicas.

cards.heading: No Police & Unequal Ranks
cards.stat: Citizens Fined vs Enslaved Workers Whipped
cards.connective: Yet Roman soldiers did not investigate everyday stolen property.
cards.html: Victims had to catch thieves themselves while vigiles watched for fires. Wealthy Roman citizens paid fines, whereas enslaved people faced harsh whipping.
cards.spoken: Yet Roman soldiers did not investigate everyday stolen property. <short pause> Victims had to catch thieves themselves while vigiles watched for fires. Wealthy Roman citizens paid fines, whereas enslaved people faced harsh whipping.

cards.heading: Bath’s Lead Curse Tablets
cards.stat: 130+ Scratched Lead Pleas at Aquae Sulis
cards.connective: When thieves escaped unseen, angry bathers asked a goddess for help.
cards.html: At steaming Aquae Sulis (Bath), robbed bathers scratched Latin pleas onto folded lead curse tablets begging Sulis Minerva to punish cloak thieves.
cards.spoken: When thieves escaped unseen, angry bathers asked a goddess for help. <short pause> At steaming Aquae Sulis (Bath), robbed bathers scratched Latin pleas onto folded lead curse tablets begging Sulis Minerva to punish cloak thieves.

cards.heading: Written Rules Without Detectives
cards.stat: Stone Courts Above, Sacred Curses Below
cards.connective: Rome proved written laws mattered, even though rank and luck shaped justice.
cards.html: Roman Britain combined clear written courts and honest market scales with unequal slave punishments and supernatural Bath curses.
cards.spoken: Rome proved written laws mattered, even though rank and luck shaped justice. <short pause> Roman Britain combined clear written courts and honest market scales with unequal slave punishments and supernatural Bath curses.

lesson_1.takeaway: Roman Britain introduced written laws and basilica magistrates, yet without police detectives victims caught thieves themselves or dropped lead curse tablets into Bath’s spring.
vocab: 1. Twelve Tables
Rome’s ancient written law code followed across the empire.
2. Magistrate
Official Roman town judge sitting inside the stone basilica.
3. Vigiles
Roman night-watchmen who spotted fires and street brawls.
lesson_1.provenanceNote: Roman Baths Museum (Bath), British Library, Ashmolean Museum (Oxford), Wellcome Collection, Metropolitan Museum of Art & Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_1.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> Roman Britain introduced written laws and basilica magistrates, yet without police detectives victims caught thieves themselves or dropped lead curse tablets into Bath’s spring.

lesson_2.topicLabel: Enquiry 02: Anglo-Saxon Tithings, Wergild and Trial by Ordeal (AD 410–1066)
lesson_2.title: Were Anglo-Saxon laws fair community rules or painful superstitions?
lesson_2.spokenTitle: Were Anglo-Saxon laws fair community rules or painful superstitions?

cards.heading: Tithings & The Hue and Cry
cards.connective: Were Anglo-Saxon laws fair community rules or painful superstitions?
cards.html: With zero police or prisons, every boy aged twelve joined a ten-person tithing. Shouting the Hue and Cry forced the whole village to chase thieves.
cards.spoken: Were Anglo-Saxon laws fair community rules or painful superstitions? <short pause> With zero police or prisons, every boy aged twelve joined a ten-person tithing. Shouting the Hue and Cry forced the whole village to chase thieves.

cards.heading: King Alfred & Silver Wergild
cards.connective: To stop deadly revenge feuds, royal law codes priced every injury in silver.
cards.html: King Alfred’s written laws enforced silver wergild ("person-price") paid to injured families — stopping blood feuds even though nobles ranked higher.
cards.spoken: To stop deadly revenge feuds, royal law codes priced every injury in silver. <short pause> King Alfred’s written laws enforced silver wergild ("person-price") paid to injured families — stopping blood feuds even though nobles ranked higher.

cards.heading: Hundred Courts & Ordeals
cards.stat: 3 Paces With Red-Hot Iron or Cold Water
cards.connective: When human witnesses could not agree, priests asked God to judge.
cards.html: If oaths at the Hundred Court deadlocked, suspects faced Trial by Ordeal in church — checking bandaged burns three days later.
cards.spoken: When human witnesses could not agree, priests asked God to judge. <short pause> If oaths at the Hundred Court deadlocked, suspects faced Trial by Ordeal in church — checking bandaged burns three days later.

cards.heading: Community Peace Mixed With Faith
cards.connective: Teamwork and compensation kept most villages calm without prisons.
cards.html: Anglo-Saxon justice blended smart neighbour tithings and peacemaking silver wergild with superstitious last-resort church ordeals.
cards.spoken: Teamwork and compensation kept most villages calm without prisons. <short pause> Anglo-Saxon justice blended smart neighbour tithings and peacemaking silver wergild with superstitious last-resort church ordeals.

lesson_2.takeaway: Anglo-Saxon villages kept peace without police using ten-person tithings, Hue and Cry chases, and silver wergild fines, turning to church Trials by Ordeal only when witnesses disagreed.
vocab: 1. Tithing
Ten neighbours aged 12+ responsible for each other’s behaviour.
2. Hue and Cry
Loud village alarm forcing everyone to chase a runaway thief.
3. Wergild
Silver "person-price" paid to victims’ families to stop feuds.
lesson_2.provenanceNote: Roman Baths Museum (Bath), British Library, Ashmolean Museum (Oxford), Wellcome Collection, Metropolitan Museum of Art & Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_2.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> Anglo-Saxon villages kept peace without police using ten-person tithings, Hue and Cry chases, and silver wergild fines, turning to church Trials by Ordeal only when witnesses disagreed.

lesson_3.topicLabel: Enquiry 03: Norman Forest Laws, Sanctuary and Royal Courts (1066–1485)
lesson_3.title: How did Norman kings and medieval royal judges change English justice after 1066?
lesson_3.spokenTitle: How did Norman kings and medieval royal judges change English justice after 1066?

cards.heading: Norman Forest Laws
cards.connective: How did Norman kings and medieval royal judges change English justice after 1066?
cards.html: After 1066, William I kept tithings yet took court fines for the Crown. Strict Forest Laws made peasant deer hunting a crime called poaching.
cards.spoken: How did Norman kings and medieval royal judges change English justice after 1066? <short pause> After 1066, William I kept tithings yet took court fines for the Crown. Strict Forest Laws made peasant deer hunting a crime called poaching.

cards.heading: Henry II’s Juries & 1215
cards.connective: Royal reforms soon replaced superstitious ordeals with evidence.
cards.html: Henry II’s travelling judges built one Common Law with twelve-person juries. In 1215, Magna Carta and the Pope’s ordeal ban cemented jury trials.
cards.spoken: Royal reforms soon replaced superstitious ordeals with evidence. <short pause> Henry II’s travelling judges built one Common Law with twelve-person juries. In 1215, Magna Carta and the Pope’s ordeal ban cemented jury trials.

cards.heading: Sanctuary, Stocks & Pillories
cards.connective: Cathedrals and market squares also shaped medieval daily justice.
cards.html: Fugitives striking Durham’s Sanctuary Knocker gained temporary Church safety, while towns shamed dishonest traders in wooden stocks and pillories.
cards.spoken: Cathedrals and market squares also shaped medieval daily justice. <short pause> Fugitives striking Durham’s Sanctuary Knocker gained temporary Church safety, while towns shamed dishonest traders in wooden stocks and pillories.

cards.heading: Birth of the English Jury Trial
cards.stat: Common Law & Magna Carta Endure Today
cards.connective: Out of harsh Norman control grew lasting fair-trial protections.
cards.html: Though Forest Laws were harsh, medieval England replaced hot-iron ordeals with Common Law judges, twelve-person juries, and Magna Carta.
cards.spoken: Out of harsh Norman control grew lasting fair-trial protections. <short pause> Though Forest Laws were harsh, medieval England replaced hot-iron ordeals with Common Law judges, twelve-person juries, and Magna Carta.

lesson_3.takeaway: Norman kings introduced harsh Forest Laws, yet medieval England also created lasting justice through Henry II’s Common Law, twelve-person juries, and 1215 Magna Carta.
vocab: 1. Forest Laws
Norman laws protecting royal hunting woods from villagers.
2. Poaching
Secretly hunting royal or lordly deer and rabbits for food.
3. Common Law
Shared English law applied by travelling judges and juries.
lesson_3.provenanceNote: Roman Baths Museum (Bath), British Library, Ashmolean Museum (Oxford), Wellcome Collection, Metropolitan Museum of Art & Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_3.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> Norman kings introduced harsh Forest Laws, yet medieval England also created lasting justice through Henry II’s Common Law, twelve-person juries, and 1215 Magna Carta.

lesson_4.topicLabel: Enquiry 04: Tudor Vagrants, High Treason and Witchcraft Trials (1485–1700)
lesson_4.title: Why did Tudor and Stuart rulers fear vagrants, plotters, and accused witches so fiercely?
lesson_4.spokenTitle: Why did Tudor and Stuart rulers fear vagrants, plotters, and accused witches so fiercely?

cards.heading: Tudor Vagrants & 1601 Poor Law
cards.stat: Sick Locals Helped vs Beggars Whipped
cards.connective: Why did Tudor and Stuart rulers fear vagrants, plotters, and accused witches so fiercely?
cards.html: Rising poverty put jobless vagrants on Tudor roads. Elizabeth I’s 1601 Poor Law helped elderly locals yet whipped healthy "sturdy beggars" behind carts.
cards.spoken: Why did Tudor and Stuart rulers fear vagrants, plotters, and accused witches so fiercely? <short pause> Rising poverty put jobless vagrants on Tudor roads. Elizabeth I’s 1601 Poor Law helped elderly locals yet whipped healthy "sturdy beggars" behind carts.

cards.heading: 1605 Gunpowder High Treason
cards.connective: Religious quarrels also made monarchs dread plots against the Crown.
cards.html: Tipped off by the Monteagle Letter on 4–5 November 1605, guards caught Guy Fawkes beside 36 gunpowder barrels and punished High Treason fiercely.
cards.spoken: Religious quarrels also made monarchs dread plots against the Crown. <short pause> Tipped off by the Monteagle Letter on 4–5 November 1605, guards caught Guy Fawkes beside 36 gunpowder barrels and punished High Treason fiercely.

cards.heading: Witch Trials Ended by Science
cards.connective: Wartime superstition peaked in 1645 before science changed minds.
cards.html: Civil War chaos let Matthew Hopkins accuse East Anglian women, until post-1660 science, strict judges, and the 1736 Act ended witch trials.
cards.spoken: Wartime superstition peaked in 1645 before science changed minds. <short pause> Civil War chaos let Matthew Hopkins accuse East Anglian women, until post-1660 science, strict judges, and the 1736 Act ended witch trials.

cards.heading: From Superstition Toward Reason
cards.stat: Real Courtroom Proof Defeated Magic Claims
cards.connective: Early modern fear brought harsh deterrence, yet science ended witch hunts.
cards.html: Without police, rulers whipped vagabonds and punished 1605 treason, while growing scientific reason banished witchcraft trials forever.
cards.spoken: Early modern fear brought harsh deterrence, yet science ended witch hunts. <short pause> Without police, rulers whipped vagabonds and punished 1605 treason, while growing scientific reason banished witchcraft trials forever.

lesson_4.takeaway: Fear of poverty, religious treason, and Civil War drove harsh Tudor-Stuart vagrancy, 1605 treason, and witch laws—until peace and 1660s science ended witch trials.
vocab: 1. Vagrant
Homeless person wandering Tudor roads looking for work or food.
2. Poor Law
1601 Elizabethan law separating sick locals from whipped beggars.
3. High Treason
Plotting against the monarch or Parliament—the gravest crime.
lesson_4.provenanceNote: Roman Baths Museum (Bath), British Library, Ashmolean Museum (Oxford), Wellcome Collection, Metropolitan Museum of Art & Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_4.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> Fear of poverty, religious treason, and Civil War drove harsh Tudor-Stuart vagrancy, 1605 treason, and witch laws—until peace and 1660s science ended witch trials.

lesson_5.topicLabel: Enquiry 05: Smugglers, Highwaymen and The Bloody Code (1700–1820)
lesson_5.title: Why did Britain pass over 200 death-penalty laws—and why did juries stop using them?
lesson_5.spokenTitle: Why did Britain pass over 200 death-penalty laws—and why did juries stop using them?

cards.heading: Smugglers & Highwaymen
cards.stat: High Tea Taxes & Lonely Turnpike Roads
cards.connective: Why did Britain pass over 200 death-penalty laws—and why did juries stop using them?
cards.html: Heavy import taxes fuelled Cornish smuggling, while unlit roads and flintlock pistols helped mounted highwaymen like Dick Turpin.
cards.spoken: Why did Britain pass over 200 death-penalty laws—and why did juries stop using them? <short pause> Heavy import taxes fuelled Cornish smuggling, while unlit roads and flintlock pistols helped mounted highwaymen like Dick Turpin.

cards.heading: The 220-Crime Bloody Code
cards.connective: Refusing to fund police, Georgian MPs relied on gallows terror.
cards.html: By 1810, stealing five shillings meant hanging under the Bloody Code — until sympathetic twelve-person juries refused to convict petty thieves.
cards.spoken: Refusing to fund police, Georgian MPs relied on gallows terror. <short pause> By 1810, stealing five shillings meant hanging under the Bloody Code — until sympathetic twelve-person juries refused to convict petty thieves.

cards.heading: Australia & Elizabeth Fry
cards.connective: New punishments and humane prison reformers soon reshaped justice.
cards.html: Britain shipped convicts via transportation to Australia (1787–1868), while Elizabeth Fry proved rehabilitation worked inside Newgate Prison.
cards.spoken: New punishments and humane prison reformers soon reshaped justice. <short pause> Britain shipped convicts via transportation to Australia (1787–1868), while Elizabeth Fry proved rehabilitation worked inside Newgate Prison.

cards.heading: Harsh Gallows Deterrence Failed
cards.connective: Cruel laws collapsed when ordinary jurors and reformers demanded fairness.
cards.html: Reluctant English juries, Australian transportation, and Elizabeth Fry’s schooling paved the way for Peel’s 1820s reforms.
cards.spoken: Cruel laws collapsed when ordinary jurors and reformers demanded fairness. <short pause> Reluctant English juries, Australian transportation, and Elizabeth Fry’s schooling paved the way for Peel’s 1820s reforms.

lesson_5.takeaway: High taxes and unlit roads sparked smuggling and highwaymen, yet Georgian MPs’ 220-crime Bloody Code failed when juries balked—leading to Australian transportation and Elizabeth Fry’s prison reforms.
vocab: 1. Smuggling
Landing untaxed tea, silk, and brandy on dark beaches at night.
2. Highwayman
Mounted pistol robber holding up coaches on lonely roads.
3. Bloody Code
Harsh Georgian laws punishing over 220 crimes by hanging.
lesson_5.provenanceNote: Roman Baths Museum (Bath), British Library, Ashmolean Museum (Oxford), Wellcome Collection, Metropolitan Museum of Art & Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_5.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> High taxes and unlit roads sparked smuggling and highwaymen, yet Georgian MPs’ 220-crime Bloody Code failed when juries balked—leading to Australian transportation and Elizabeth Fry’s prison reforms.

lesson_6.topicLabel: Enquiry 06: Peel’s 1829 Bobbies, Victorian Prisons and Forensics (1829–Present)
lesson_6.title: How have uniformed police, prison reform, and forensic science transformed justice since 1829?
lesson_6.spokenTitle: How have uniformed police, prison reform, and forensic science transformed justice since 1829?

cards.heading: Peel’s 1829 "Bobbies"
cards.connective: How have uniformed police, prison reform, and forensic science transformed justice since 1829?
cards.html: In 1829, Sir Robert Peel founded London’s Metropolitan Police in blue coats with wooden truncheons — preventing crime by public consent.
cards.spoken: How have uniformed police, prison reform, and forensic science transformed justice since 1829? <short pause> In 1829, Sir Robert Peel founded London’s Metropolitan Police in blue coats with wooden truncheons — preventing crime by public consent.

cards.heading: Pentonville to Ending Hanging
cards.connective: Prisons replaced transportation and eventually ended executions.
cards.html: Victorian Pentonville (1842) used solitary cells and treadwheels. Later Britain abolished murder executions in 1965 to focus on rehabilitation.
cards.spoken: Prisons replaced transportation and eventually ended executions. <short pause> Victorian Pentonville (1842) used solitary cells and treadwheels. Later Britain abolished murder executions in 1965 to focus on rehabilitation.

cards.heading: 1901 Fingerprints & 1984 DNA
cards.connective: Forensic science replaced guesswork with microscopic proof.
cards.html: 1901 fingerprints, 999 calls, CCTV, and Sir Alec Jeffreys’s 1984 DNA profiling catch offenders, clear the innocent, and fight cyber-crime.
cards.spoken: Forensic science replaced guesswork with microscopic proof. <short pause> 1901 fingerprints, 999 calls, CCTV, and Sir Alec Jeffreys’s 1984 DNA profiling catch offenders, clear the innocent, and fight cyber-crime.

cards.heading: Science, Prevention & Fair Rights
cards.connective: Two thousand years combined medieval jury rights with modern science.
cards.html: Modern Britain pairs twelve-person juries and unarmed policing with rehabilitation and DNA forensics.
cards.spoken: Two thousand years combined medieval jury rights with modern science. <short pause> Modern Britain pairs twelve-person juries and unarmed policing with rehabilitation and DNA forensics.

lesson_6.takeaway: Since 1829, Peel’s unarmed Bobbies, prison reform ending hanging in 1965, 1901 fingerprints, and 1984 Leicester DNA profiling have transformed British justice.
vocab: 1. Peelers
1829 uniformed London police founded by Sir Robert Peel.
2. Policing by Consent
Policing peacefully with citizens’ trust rather than army guns.
3. Separate System
Victorian Pentonville plan keeping prisoners silent and alone.

lesson_6.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> Since 1829, Peel’s unarmed Bobbies, prison reform ending hanging in 1965, 1901 fingerprints, and 1984 Leicester DNA profiling have transformed British justice.
